title: A Spreading Family, a Secure City (Isaiah 54)
transcript: Well, for those of us who have been following this series for some time, we are now coming to the last two chapters in this series. Last week in Isaiah 53 we reached something of the climax from chapter 40 to 55 with the picture of the servant of the Lord—you will remember if you were here—who is in fact the arm of the Lord, the Lord himself, pointing to our Lord Jesus Christ, God himself in human flesh who bore our sins and died for our salvation and was raised again. All of that is accomplished in chapter 53. And what we have now in chapter 54 and 55, the last two chapters, are basically a command and an invitation. The command in chapter 54 is to sing and rejoice as we have been doing. And the invitation in chapter 55 is 'Come, come and enjoy a feast.' And next week we will be looking at that with Olly Lansdown. I hope you will come back for that next week. So our chapter really has two halves. In verses 1-10 we see that love wins and in verses 11-17 that peace reigns, or will reign ultimately. So first of all then, love wins. As I said at the very beginning, Jerusalem is portrayed here as a people, but they are portrayed as a wife who is both childless and abandoned. It is a very stark description of the reality of the city of Jerusalem at that time and of the people who were in exile in Babylon and had been for two generations. And in fact, that is exactly how they thought of themselves. Because in chapter 49 they were saying, "The Lord has forsaken me, the Lord has forgotten me." They just feel abandoned and, as a sense, no more future, no possibility of children. But here at the beginning in this verse, this childless wife is jumping for joy. "Sing, rejoice"—there are three verbs here which are really emphatic—"shout for joy." Now surely, surely, 'Well, to tell a wife who has had no children to shout for joy is cruel.' Well, yes, of course it is, except for what follows in the second half of the verse, which is that God promises that she will have so many children that she is going to have to build a bigger tent, strengthen the stakes, lengthen the cords, get more canvas. There is going to need more room, more elbow room for all the children who are coming along. Those verses, verses 2 and 3—can you see them there?—are very much a reminder to the people of Israel, the exiles in Babylon, of the promises that God had made to Abraham right away back at the beginning. There are a lot of echoes. After all, Abraham, you remember, had a childless wife, Sarah. They were living in tents and God promised them that they would have descendants like stars in the sky and sand on the seashore—a promise that God would renew renewed to Jacob, the grandson of Abraham, when he said to him, "Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth. You will spread out to the west and the east, the north and the south, and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you and your offspring." And that promise is here being renewed to this childless woman portrayed as Israel. You are going to have all these descendants. And that, of course, was true, not only in the sense that Israel, the people of the Old Testament, survived, returned to Jerusalem, and continued to grow, but of course, that through the gospel, as we now know, and we are proof of it sitting here in this room, that God's worldwide family in Jesus Christ is actually the largest family on earth. And we get to be part of it, to be part of the fulfillment of this promise, that we are among those where the gospel has spread. And then, of course, at the even longer horizon, as I said, the third horizon, the ultimate, it is the book of Revelation where John says that he says, "I saw a great multitude that no one could count from every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before the throne of God and before the Lamb," in Revelation 7:9. 'before the Lamb.' Who was that? Well, of course, that was the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. That's the one who went as a lamb to the slaughter in chapter 53, none other than the servant of the Lord himself. So here is this opening picture of the passage—childless wife jumping for joy because there is going to be a worldwide family that will follow. But love wins also because, as we see secondly, that there is going to be a broken marriage that is healed by love. And that is in verses 4 to 10. Now in our culture and our world today, not having children may or may not be a matter of sadness, of grief, of disappointment. But whatever it is, it is nothing to be ashamed of. But in the world of Israel way back then, a childless wife lived a life of deep shame, pain, contempt. This was of course before anybody knew the fact that infertility might be the man's problem, not just the woman's.. But in those days it was the woman who would be blamed if there were no children. And that blame would lead to scorn and mockery and provoking and all of the bitterness that would come with it. I mean, ask Hannah in the Bible, the mother of Samuel, if you want to know how that felt. But for the exiles, the shame aspect of this, which is there in the text, was far deeper. Because it was the shame of all that adulterous unfaithfulness to God that had been part of their, quote, "marriage" for centuries. You see, in the Old Testament picture of God and the people, Yahweh and Israel, it was described like a covenant of marriage. But as the prophets show us, for centuries Israel, this people, this wife, as it were, of the Lord himself. They had gone off after countless other lovers, other gods, other nations, other alliances, other idols. And the result was this wrenching, broken, shattered marriage in the picture language of the text. There had not been any formal divorce as such. That is what we read in chapter 50, verse 1, where God says, "Where is the certificate of divorce? I haven't divorced you." But it had been a painful, agonizing separation. And it was a separation under God's judgment—right, proper, deserved, and justified. And that is what the exile had been—well, still was in the time of this text—a broken, shattered marriage in tatters. And look what verse 6 says. He says it is a bit like the wife of your youth who was precious and loved, the sort of honeymoon period, but it turns out that she is actually adulterous and gone off with other lovers. And you could ask Hosea how that felt, if you like. But, says God— can you see there in verse 7? God says, "It was only for a brief moment." We say, "Excuse me, Lord, It had been 70 years. Two whole generations the exile lasted. Brief moment? Well, yes, but you see, in God's calendar, in God's diary, we are told, 1,000 years are like one day. So 70 years is just a few minutes, a brief moment. And that way of talking about God's anger, in fact, is picked up in Psalm 30:5 where where we read, "Sing the praises of the Lord, you his faithful people, for his anger lasts only a moment, but his favor lasts a lifetime. Weeping may stay for the night, but rejoicing comes in the morning." And that is, in a sense, the imbalance between God's anger, which was real, and his long-term, lifelong, and eternal grace and favor that he is bringing back to them. So yes, it was God's anger, truly unjustified. But as the text said, it was saturated, it was embraced within God's love and compassion. Do you see there in verses 7 and 8, "With deep compassion," literally great mercies, it is plural, "great compassion I will bring you back." And then verse 8, "With Everlasting kindness, love, faithfulness—that is the character of God. Anger, yes, but love. These days, of course, some people are inclined to ask, "Well, how can a loving God be angry?" I think actually a better question would be, "How could a loving God not be angry?" When the object of his love, the person he truly loves, is engaged in radical self-harm and destructive loss, both self-abuse and being abused by others, when someone God loves is being treated like that and they are behaving like that, surely God is going to be angry about that, isn't he? And that is exactly what this text is telling us. I remember sitting at our dining room table, Liz my wife and I, with a woman whose husband had been behaving in very strange and rather unpleasant and bad ways. And she, the woman in question, she was visibly angry about this, as we were. And the anger was coming out. But then through her tears she said, "But I still love him and I want him back." And if that anger and love can be there in one human heart, That is exactly what God is saying here in verse 6. He has gone through the anger of all the betrayal and loss and adultery, "But the Lord will call you back," it says in verse 6. That is what he is going to do—call you back. It is almost as if God is saying, you know, "Let's have a renewal, as it were, of our wedding vows. Let's have a fresh," as it were, almost like a second wedding. In fact, in verse 5 that is sort of how it says, "Your Maker is your husband." So let's picture this. Here is Yahweh, the living God, the bridegroom. And here is Israel, the blushing bride, blushing with joy because there is restoration but also perhaps blushing with shame because of the past. And imagine them there, as it were, and we are coming as we do in weddings to the signing of the register, okay? And we say, "Okay, bride, what name shall we write?" "Well, Israel actually. Nothing much else. House of Jacob maybe? Can we get that in?" "Yeah, okay. And you, sir, husband, what would you like to be here?" 'Well, you are a maker actually, Israel. It is not just that you are my wife; I actually made you in the first place.' Okay, you are a maker. 'Oh, and also the Lord Almighty, you see,' which actually means the Lord of hosts, 'because I am the Lord of all the heavenly armies, the angels, the archangels, all the company of heaven, and I want them to be here too, if they will fit in the church.' 'Well, no. I am also the Holy One of Israel. I am the one who has made this woman to be holy, to be clean and pure as I am. That is what I want her to be for me as well.' Holy One of Israel—is that it? 'Well, no. You are Redeemer.' 'Because I think you will find that I am the one who bought you for myself, brought you out of Egypt in the Exodus, bought you with my own blood through my Son Jesus Christ, your Redeemer.' Are we finished? There is not much room here. Well, why don't you just put down 'God of all the earth'? That will do it. Can you see, verse 5, what is happening? That list, isn't it amazing? "Your Maker, the Lord Almighty, the Holy One of Israel, your Redeemer, the God of all the earth." I mean, what a husband! What a husband! "This is your husband," he says. This is the God who is claiming Israel here in this text. As his wife. And this is who we are married to if we are in Christ, because we are the bride of Christ, as the Bible will say later on in its imagery. This, this is the God who created us, who loved us, who redeemed us, who died for us, who brought us back out of sin and rebellion and slavery and death. And this is the God who signs a covenant of marriage with us as his bride. Love wins is what is happening in this chapter. And indeed, if we carry this right forward to the very end of the Scripture, this is how the Bible ends. It is a happy ending. Because at the end of the book, the lover wins his girl, the beloved. And the end of the Bible is a marriage. Love wins. And this marriage made in heaven is consummated on earth in the new heaven and the new earth, which are now united as one creation, one new creation, just as the bride and the groom, the heavenly bridegroom and his bride, Christ and the church, are united as one. That's where this story is going ultimately. And speaking of the earth, this is a marriage which is even more durable and more lasting than the earth itself, because that's what comes in verses 9 and 10. You see there where God suddenly decides this is a bit, to me he says, a bit like the days of Noah when God after the flood had promised that never again would he judge the earth in that way with the flood. And now he is saying that never again And then will I act in rage or in anger or in judgment or condemnation? No, this love is going to be more durable even than the mountains of the earth. The mountains may pass away, literally walk off is the picture. The mountains may walk off, but my love, my compassion, my unfailing love for you will never be broken. Never again for all eternity. Why not? Well, again, because of chapter 53, because God himself has borne our sin and our wanderings and our evil, and that has been borne by Christ. And that is why, therefore, the climax of all things in heaven and earth in the Scripture is ultimately the eternal love of God for his people,. And the invitation goes out to all of us to join that wedding feast. You see, here is what it says in Revelation chapter 19 before that great wedding banquet happens. It says, "Let us rejoice and be glad and give him glory, for the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready." And then the angel said to me, "Write this: Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb." And he added, "These are the true words of God." I wonder if you responded to that wedding invitation. See, it is a bit rude, isn't it, if you are invited to a wedding and you don't even bother to reply? It is even more rude if you refuse to go for no real reason. And here you are invited to the wedding of Christ and his people, to be part of the party. What I want to urge is don't miss that. Don't miss out on the greatest wedding party in the universe. Love wins. And the question is whether God's love for you has won you yet to be part of his bride in this wonderful picture that the Bible gives us. So that's the first, love wins. But we need to move on a little bit more briefly to peace reigns in verses 11 to 17. Peace reigns. The imagery changes, but it's still female. Now we are thinking about a city being addressed by God as you. But it is "you," feminine singular. This is a city that is being described. And of course it means originally Jerusalem back in the Old Testament. And it is a ruined city that has to be rebuilt. And that is what we have there. You can see very clearly in verses 11 to 12 that God promises that this city which is afflicted, lashed, tossed by the storm and the sea, not comforted—that was the reality, of course, of Jerusalem all through the years of the exile. In fact, immediately after the destruction of the city in 587 BC, this is from the book of Lamentations, the first few verses: How deserted lies the city, once so full of people! But how like a widow she is now! She who was once great among the nations, now was a queen among the provinces, now become a slave. 'Bitterly she weeps at night; tears are on her cheeks. And among all her lovers there is no one to comfort her.' Which, as we have been seeing, is what these chapters are all about, is bringing comfort back to the people. And of course, at the level of the Old Testament, this happened. God promised that the exiles would return, that the city would be rebuilt. That it would be beautiful again, perhaps not quite as dazzlingly beautiful as these verses describe. After the exile we have got Nehemiah and Ezra and so on in that period. But remember that the city was more than just buildings; it was also the people, the people who filled the city and had turned it into a place of rebels. This is what Isaiah chapter 1 says about the city of Jerusalem: "How the faithful city has become like a prostitute, The one that was full of justice, righteousness used to be there, but now it is full of murderers and rebels and thieves. But, says God, same chapter, verse 26, "Afterwards you will be called the city of righteousness and the faithful people." So God is promising that he is going to give rebuilding to this ruined, broken city. But if that was going to happen, then something else would happen in verse 13, that the rebellious citizens of the city would need to be discipled. "All your children," it says there— can you see it? "All your children will be taught by the Lord." And children, of course, doesn't mean kids. It is not a Sunday school. The children are simply the citizens of the city. And they are going to be taught by the Lord. They will be disciples of God, just like the servant is described in chapter 50, that he would be one who would be listening to the word of the Lord. So only when there is true knowledge of God, when there is obedience to God's ways, being taught by the Lord, righteousness in action, will there be peace. That is the word there as you can see it. You will be given peace in verse 13. Great will be their peace. The word, of course, I am sure many of us know is the Hebrew word shalom. It means not just the absence of war or conflict. It means total well-being, all that we are meant to be as God. And it's a wonderfully big theme in Isaiah. But not— look at all of these texts, there isn't time, but it runs all the way through. The child born in chapter 9 will be the Prince of Peace. God will give perfect peace to those who trust him in chapter 26. You will establish peace for us in verse 12. The Spirit of the Lord will be poured out in chapter 32, bringing justice and righteousness and peace. Here in this chapter, 54:10, there will be a covenant of peace with the city, and great will be their peace in verse 13. All the way through, God wants us to have peace, that peace will reign. But how is that going to happen? And if you look on the same page, right at the top of page 742, you will see the reason. And that is in Isaiah 53:5: He was pierced, the servant Christ was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities, And the punishment that brought us peace was upon him, and by his wounds we are healed. And so again, all that this chapter is talking about—love wins, peace will reign—it comes because of what God has done for us in Christ. And that leads us to the last part of the chapter, that peace will reign because the servants of God, God's righteous servants, will be protected. Verses 14 to 17. Do you notice there in verse 14 that it says, sorry, in verse 17 it speaks about the servants of the Lord. The servants are now plural. Up to this point in Isaiah, the servant has always been singular, either the people of Israel as God's servant or the servant of the Lord who would come to bring salvation. But from this point on to the very end of the book, it is not plural. It is servants. It is the people, those who are in the Lord Jesus Christ, and that is us. And so God's servants, says verse 14, are going to be established in righteousness. They will therefore, because of that, have nothing to fear. You will have nothing to fear. And we say, "What? Really?" I mean, surely from this point on through the whole history of the Jewish people and of the Christian people, there have been stacks of things to fear. These people were still going to go through the Persian Empire, the Greek Empire, the Roman Empire, and then on through the persecutions of the following centuries. There is so much to fear in the world. But, says God, it is not going to be because of my judgment. God is not against his people from this point on. As we were singing earlier, "If God is for us, who can be against us?" which of course is a quotation from the book of Romans. Indeed, says verse 16, God himself not only controls the people who may attack his people, but he is also the creator of the breath of the blacksmith who blows the fire who makes the weapon that is in the hand of the soldier who may be attacking God's people. It is a marvelous composite picture in verse 16. And what it is basically saying is that nothing that happens to God's people will be either outside of God's ultimate control or ultimately destroy them, whether it is violent attack, or false accusation, one way or another, God will make sure of verse 17 that no weapon forged against you will prevail and no word that is spoken—refute every tongue that accuses you. That is God's safeguarding policy. That is God's promise to his people. But can we really believe it? It doesn't mean that there is going to be no weapons. It doesn't mean there is going to be no false accusations. God's people have endured such things all through the centuries, but they will not prevail against them, says God, even those who suffer the most unjust deaths and destruction. Some of us quite recently were reading a book by Alex Navalny, who was the Russian patriot. He was the leader of the opposition against the Kremlin and Vladimir Putin in the 2010s. They attempted to poison him in 2020, but he survived and recovered in Germany. And then in 2021, just 3 years ago, he went back to Russia. He was arrested on arrival and imprisoned and went through 3 years of incredible suffering in prison. And I just thought I would read you a couple of things he says about the sort of accusations that he had to face up to. He said this, I'm quoting, "Some people collect stamps, some people collect coins. I have a growing collection of court trials. I was tried in a police station, I was tried in a standard regime penal colony, now they're trying me in a closed trial in a maximum security penal colony." And he goes on, "They initiate a new criminal case against me every 3 months." Rarely has an inmate in solitary confinement for more than a year had such a vibrant social, political, and criminal life. He maintained his sense of humor. But he was also a believer, and this is where I wanted to end because this is what he says. He says at the very end, the last page of the book, he says, I've always thought and said openly that being a believer makes life easier. Faith makes life simpler. He says, you lie in your bunk looking up and you ask yourself whether you are a Christian in your heart of hearts. Are you a disciple of the one who sacrificed himself for others, paying the price of their sins? If you can honestly answer yes, then what is there left for you to worry about? And then he says these words, the last words of the book: "My job is to seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness and leave it to good old Jesus and the rest of his family to deal with everything else." I love that—good old Jesus. You see, Navalny knew that that the final word in his case did not rest with the Kremlin but with good old Jesus, with God, the ultimate judge, who would defend his innocence and his vindication. And that's what verse 17 means for us. That's what God guarantees us. That's what this verse means, that this is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord. This is their righteousness from me, declares the Lord. Our future is guaranteed by God himself. Love wins and there will be eternal peace. So Isaiah 54 then, it is a wonderful chapter. It is a chapter with a bride and with a city. And how fitting it is that at the end of the Bible what John says he sees is, "I saw the holy city, the New Jerusalem, coming down from heaven out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride, a city that was a bride dressed beautifully for her husband. And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, 'Look, God's dwelling place is now among the people. He will dwell with them. They will be his people. God will be with them and be their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. No more death, no more mourning or crying or pain, for all the old things have passed away.' So you see, it invites us to rejoice because in the end love wins and peace will reign. And is that what you know? Is that what you believe? Are you certain of that for yourself? It is for anyone who puts their faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. And if it is true, then as the bride of Christ you are loved with an everlasting love. And as the citizen of the city of God you are safe with everlasting peace. May God help us to grasp these truths and go out and rejoice in them this night. Let's pray together. And as I pray, the band will come up for our final song together. O God, we thank you for the words of your prophet. We thank you for giving him such rich visions of your purposes and plans, of your love and compassion and kindness and goodness. Please help us, Lord, to realize that we are loved with an eternal love and that we are safe with eternal peace once we have put ourselves into the hands of God and trusted in the Lord Jesus Christ. For your name's sake. Amen.
